questions.s: The mass of 0.25 mol of carbon dioxide is (C = 12, O = 16)
questions.e: Molar mass of CO₂ = 12 + 2 × 16 = 44 g mol⁻¹, so mass = 0.25 × 44 = 11 g. 7 g comes from using 28 g mol⁻¹ (carbon monoxide), and 176 g comes from dividing 44 by 0.25 instead of multiplying.

questions.s: How many atoms in total are present in 0.5 mol of water, H₂O? (NA = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
questions.e: 0.5 mol of H₂O contains 0.5 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 3.01 × 10²³ molecules, and each molecule has 3 atoms, giving 9.03 × 10²³ atoms. 3.01 × 10²³ counts molecules only, and 6.02 × 10²³ counts only the hydrogen atoms.

questions.s: The volume occupied by 32 g of methane, CH₄, at STP is (C = 12, H = 1; molar volume = 22.4 dm³ mol⁻¹)
questions.e: Molar mass of CH₄ = 12 + 4 = 16 g mol⁻¹, so 32 g is 2 mol, and 2 × 22.4 = 44.8 dm³. 22.4 dm³ assumes 32 g is one mole, which is true for O₂, not for CH₄.

questions.s: A compound contains 40.0 % carbon, 6.7 % hydrogen and 53.3 % oxygen by mass. Its empirical formula is (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
questions.e: Divide each percentage by the atomic mass: C 40/12 = 3.33, H 6.7/1 = 6.7, O 53.3/16 = 3.33. Dividing by the smallest (3.33) gives C : H : O = 1 : 2 : 1, so CH₂O. CH₂O₂ comes from dividing oxygen by 8 instead of 16.

questions.s: A hydrocarbon has the empirical formula CH and a molar mass of 78 g mol⁻¹. Its molecular formula is (C = 12, H = 1)
questions.e: Empirical formula mass of CH = 13, and 78/13 = 6, so the molecular formula is (CH)₆ = C₆H₆, benzene. C₂H₂ (ethyne) has the same empirical formula but a molar mass of only 26.

questions.s: 4 g of hydrogen gas is reacted with 16 g of oxygen gas: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. The mass of water formed is (H = 1, O = 16)
questions.e: H₂ = 4/2 = 2 mol and O₂ = 16/32 = 0.5 mol. 2 mol H₂ would need 1 mol O₂, so O₂ is limiting; 0.5 mol O₂ gives 1 mol H₂O = 18 g. 36 g wrongly takes hydrogen as the limiting reactant.

questions.s: Which of the following contains the largest number of molecules? (H = 1, C = 12, O = 16)
questions.e: Moles: H₂ 1/2 = 0.5, O₂ 16/32 = 0.5, CO₂ 22/44 = 0.5, H₂O 18/18 = 1. The sample with the most moles has the most molecules, so 18 g of water. Choosing 22 g of CO₂ because it has the largest mass ignores molar mass.

questions.s: Ali heats 10 g of calcium carbonate strongly: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. He obtains 4.2 g of calcium oxide. The percentage yield is (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)
questions.e: 10 g CaCO₃ = 10/100 = 0.1 mol, which should give 0.1 mol CaO = 5.6 g. Percentage yield = 4.2/5.6 × 100 = 75 %. 56 % is the theoretical mass of CaO mistaken for the yield.

questions.s: The mass of oxygen present in 0.2 mol of sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃, is (O = 16)
questions.e: Each Na₂CO₃ has 3 oxygen atoms, so 0.2 mol contains 0.6 mol O atoms, and 0.6 × 16 = 9.6 g. 3.2 g counts only one oxygen atom per formula unit, and 19.2 g treats the oxygen as O₂ molecules.

questions.s: A mixture of iodine crystals and sand is best separated by
questions.e: Iodine passes directly from solid to vapour on gentle heating and re-solidifies on a cold surface, while sand stays behind, so sublimation separates them. Filtration fails because neither solid dissolves in water, and iodine is only very slightly soluble in water, so water extraction is poor.

questions.s: In a paper chromatography experiment, a dye spot moves 3.0 cm from the base line while the solvent front moves 12.0 cm. The Rf value of the dye is
questions.e: Rf = distance moved by solute / distance moved by solvent = 3.0/12.0 = 0.25. The value 4.0 inverts the ratio; Rf can never exceed 1 because a solute cannot travel further than the solvent.

questions.s: For solvent extraction of an organic compound from its aqueous solution, the chosen solvent must be one that
o: mixes completely with water and dissolves the solute well
is immiscible with water and dissolves the solute better
boils above 100 °C and is always denser than water
reacts with the solute to form a salt soluble in water
questions.e: Extraction works by distribution between two layers, so the solvent must not mix with water and the solute must be more soluble in it than in water (for example ether). A solvent that mixes with water gives no separate layer, and boiling point or density does not decide whether extraction works.

questions.s: A gas has a density of 1.25 g dm⁻³ at STP. Its molar mass is (molar volume = 22.4 dm³ mol⁻¹)
questions.e: Molar mass = density × molar volume = 1.25 × 22.4 = 28 g mol⁻¹ (for example N₂ or CO). Dividing instead of multiplying gives a meaningless small number, and 56 doubles the correct value.

questions.s: Relative atomic masses of elements are measured on a scale based on
o: one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom
the mass of one atom of hydrogen-1
one-sixteenth of the mass of an oxygen-16 atom
the mass of one proton at rest
questions.e: The modern scale defines 1 amu (atomic mass unit) as one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom, so C-12 is exactly 12. Hydrogen and oxygen scales were used historically but are no longer the standard.

questions.s: 28 g of nitrogen and 9 g of hydrogen are mixed and react completely: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. Which reactant is left over, and how much? (H = 1, N = 14)
questions.e: N₂ = 28/28 = 1 mol and H₂ = 9/2 = 4.5 mol. 1 mol N₂ uses 3 mol H₂, so N₂ is limiting and 1.5 mol H₂ remains, which is 1.5 × 2 = 3 g. 1.5 g confuses moles with grams.

questions.s: The number of moles in 4.9 g of sulphuric acid, H₂SO₄, is (H = 1, O = 16, S = 32)
questions.e: Molar mass of H₂SO₄ = 2 + 32 + 64 = 98 g mol⁻¹, so n = 4.9/98 = 0.05 mol. 0.5 mol comes from slipping a decimal place, and 0.02 mol uses 245 or another wrong molar mass.

questions.s: Complete combustion of 0.30 g of a hydrocarbon gives 0.88 g of CO₂ and 0.54 g of H₂O. The empirical formula of the hydrocarbon is (H = 1, C = 12, O = 16)
questions.e: Mass of C = 0.88 × 12/44 = 0.24 g (0.02 mol); mass of H = 0.54 × 2/18 = 0.06 g (0.06 mol). These add to 0.30 g, and C : H = 0.02 : 0.06 = 1 : 3, so CH₃ (the molecule is C₂H₆). Forgetting that each H₂O has two H atoms gives 1 : 1.5, which leads to wrong formulas such as CH₂.

questions.s: The total number of ions present in 0.05 mol of calcium chloride, CaCl₂, is (NA = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
questions.e: Each CaCl₂ gives one Ca²⁺ and two Cl⁻, so 0.05 mol gives 0.15 mol of ions; 0.15 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 9.03 × 10²². 3.01 × 10²² counts formula units, 6.02 × 10²² counts only the Cl⁻ ions, and 9.03 × 10²³ slips a power of ten.

questions.s: Impure benzoic acid is dissolved in the minimum amount of hot water, the hot solution is filtered, and the filtrate is allowed to cool so that pure solid separates out. This technique is called
questions.e: Benzoic acid is much more soluble in hot water than in cold, so it separates as pure crystals on cooling while soluble impurities stay in the mother liquor: this is crystallisation. The filtering step only removes insoluble impurities; it is not the main technique.

questions.s: Aluminium reacts with excess hydrochloric acid: 2Al + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂. The volume of hydrogen at STP produced by 5.4 g of aluminium is (Al = 27; molar volume = 22.4 dm³ mol⁻¹)
questions.e: 5.4/27 = 0.2 mol Al, and the ratio Al : H₂ is 2 : 3, giving 0.3 mol H₂ = 0.3 × 22.4 = 6.72 dm³. 4.48 dm³ assumes a 1 : 1 ratio, and 13.44 dm³ uses 3 : 1.

questions.s: A gas occupies 2.0 dm³ at 1.0 atm. At constant temperature it is compressed to 0.50 dm³. Its new pressure is
questions.e: Boyle's law: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂, so P₂ = 1.0 × 2.0/0.50 = 4.0 atm. 0.25 atm comes from inverting the ratio; the volume fell to a quarter, so the pressure must rise four times.

questions.s: A gas occupies 300 cm³ at 27 °C. At constant pressure it is heated to 127 °C. Its new volume is
questions.e: Charles's law needs kelvin: T₁ = 300 K, T₂ = 400 K, so V₂ = 300 × 400/300 = 400 cm³. Using Celsius gives 300 × 127/27 ≈ 1411 cm³, and 225 cm³ inverts the temperature ratio.

questions.s: Under the same conditions, the ratio of the rate of diffusion of hydrogen to that of oxygen is (H = 1, O = 16)
questions.e: Graham's law: rate ∝ 1/√M, so rate(H₂)/rate(O₂) = √(32/2) = √16 = 4, giving 4 : 1. 16 : 1 forgets the square root, and 1 : 4 has the lighter gas slower, which is backwards.

questions.s: A cylinder contains 0.2 mol of nitrogen and 0.3 mol of oxygen at a total pressure of 1.0 atm. The partial pressure of oxygen is
questions.e: Dalton's law: p(O₂) = mole fraction × total pressure = 0.3/(0.2 + 0.3) × 1.0 = 0.6 atm. 0.3 atm uses the number of moles as if it were the pressure, and 0.4 atm is the partial pressure of nitrogen.

questions.s: H₂O is a liquid at room temperature while H₂S is a gas. The main reason is that
o: H₂O has a larger molar mass than H₂S
H₂O molecules are hydrogen bonded to one another
H₂S molecules are non-polar and linear in shape
O–H covalent bonds are stronger than S–H bonds
questions.e: Oxygen is small and highly electronegative, so water molecules form strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds that must be broken on boiling; sulphur cannot do this. H₂O (18) is lighter than H₂S (34), and boiling breaks intermolecular forces, not the covalent bonds inside molecules.

questions.s: The number of moles of an ideal gas that occupies 8.21 dm³ at 2.0 atm and 400 K is (R = 0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
questions.e: n = PV/RT = (2.0 × 8.21)/(0.0821 × 400) = 16.42/32.84 = 0.50 mol. Turning the expression upside down (RT/PV) gives 2.0, which is not a number of moles.

questions.s: According to the kinetic molecular theory, the average kinetic energy of the molecules of a gas is directly proportional to its
questions.e: Kinetic theory gives average KE = (3/2)kT, so it depends only on the kelvin temperature. At the same temperature all gases have the same average KE whatever their molar mass; heavier molecules simply move more slowly.

questions.s: Real gases show the greatest deviation from ideal behaviour at
questions.e: At high pressure the molecules are crowded, so their own volume is no longer negligible, and at low temperature they move slowly, so intermolecular attractions matter. Low pressure and high temperature is exactly where gases behave most ideally.

questions.s: Water boils at a lower temperature in Murree than in Karachi because at higher altitude
o: the vapour pressure of water is greater
the hydrogen bonds in water are weaker
less heat reaches the water from the flame
the external atmospheric pressure is lower
questions.e: A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure. Air pressure is lower at altitude, so water reaches that vapour pressure at a lower temperature. Hydrogen bonding in water does not change with altitude.

questions.s: All crystalline solids are classified, on the basis of their unit cell dimensions and angles, into how many crystal systems?
questions.e: There are seven crystal systems: cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic, monoclinic, hexagonal, rhombohedral and triclinic. 14 is the number of Bravais lattices, which subdivides these seven systems.

questions.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
questions.e: In diamond every carbon atom is covalently bonded to four others in a giant network. Iodine is a molecular solid held by London forces, sodium chloride is ionic, and copper is metallic.

questions.s: Under identical conditions, a gas X diffuses at half the rate of methane (CH₄, molar mass 16 g mol⁻¹). The molar mass of X is
questions.e: Graham's law: rate(X)/rate(CH₄) = √(16/M) = 1/2, so 16/M = 1/4 and M = 64 g mol⁻¹. 32 g mol⁻¹ forgets to square the ratio, and smaller values would make X diffuse faster than methane.

questions.s: Which liquid has the highest vapour pressure at 25 °C?
questions.e: Diethyl ether has no O–H group, so its molecules cannot hydrogen bond to each other and escape easily, giving the highest vapour pressure. Glycerol, with three O–H groups per molecule, has the strongest hydrogen bonding and the lowest vapour pressure.

questions.s: A sample of gas occupies 500 cm³ at 27 °C and 1 atm. Its volume at 327 °C and 2 atm will be
questions.e: V₂ = V₁ × (P₁/P₂) × (T₂/T₁) = 500 × (1/2) × (600/300) = 500 cm³: doubling the pressure halves the volume and doubling the kelvin temperature doubles it back. 1000 cm³ ignores the pressure change, and 3028 cm³ uses Celsius temperatures.

questions.s: A flask contains 4 g of hydrogen and 32 g of oxygen at the same temperature. The ratio of the partial pressure of hydrogen to that of oxygen is (H = 1, O = 16)
questions.e: Partial pressure is proportional to the number of moles: H₂ = 4/2 = 2 mol and O₂ = 32/32 = 1 mol, so p(H₂) : p(O₂) = 2 : 1. 1 : 8 is the mass ratio, which does not decide pressure.

questions.s: The neutron was discovered in 1932 by bombarding beryllium with alpha particles. The scientist who discovered it was
questions.e: Chadwick showed that the penetrating radiation from beryllium consisted of neutral particles with a mass close to that of the proton: the neutron. Thomson discovered the electron, and Rutherford discovered the nucleus.

questions.s: In Rutherford's gold foil experiment, most alpha particles passed straight through the foil. This showed that
o: most of the atom is empty space
questions.e: Undeflected passage of most alpha particles means the atom is mostly empty, with its mass and positive charge concentrated in a tiny nucleus that deflected only a few particles. Fixed electron orbits were Bohr's later idea, not a result of this experiment.

questions.s: The radius of the first Bohr orbit of hydrogen is 0.529 Å. The radius of its second orbit is
questions.e: In Bohr's model rₙ = 0.529 n² Å, so r₂ = 0.529 × 4 = 2.116 Å. 1.058 Å multiplies by n instead of n², and smaller values would put the second orbit inside the first.

questions.s: The energy of the electron in the first orbit of a hydrogen atom is −13.6 eV. Its energy in the third orbit is
questions.e: Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV, so E₃ = −13.6/9 = −1.51 eV. −4.53 eV divides by n instead of n². The energy becomes less negative as n increases because the electron is less tightly bound.

questions.s: The Balmer series of the hydrogen spectrum arises from electron transitions that end in the orbit with
questions.e: Balmer lines are produced when electrons fall from n = 3, 4, 5 … to n = 2, and they lie in the visible region. Transitions ending at n = 1 form the Lyman (ultraviolet) series, and those ending at n = 3 form the Paschen (infrared) series.

questions.s: The maximum number of electrons that can be accommodated in the shell with n = 3 is
questions.e: The maximum is 2n² = 2 × 9 = 18 (3s², 3p⁶, 3d¹⁰). The number 8 is the familiar count for the third period, where 3d is not yet filled, and 32 is the capacity of n = 4.

questions.s: Which set of quantum numbers is not possible for an electron?
questions.e: l can take values from 0 to n − 1, so for n = 2 the largest allowed l is 1; l = 2 is impossible. In the other sets l < n and m lies between −l and +l, so they are all allowed.

questions.s: The number of orbitals in a d subshell is
questions.e: For a d subshell l = 2, so m takes 2l + 1 = 5 values (−2 to +2), giving five orbitals. 10 is the number of electrons a d subshell can hold, not the number of orbitals.

questions.s: The ground-state electronic configuration of chromium (Z = 24) is
questions.e: Chromium is an exception: a half-filled 3d⁵ subshell with 4s¹ is more stable than 3d⁴ 4s², so the configuration is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹. [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s² is what simple Aufbau filling predicts, but it is not the observed ground state.

questions.s: A ground-state nitrogen atom has three unpaired electrons, one in each 2p orbital. This arrangement is explained by
questions.e: Hund's rule says electrons occupy degenerate orbitals singly, with parallel spins, before pairing begins, so 2p³ has three unpaired electrons. Pauli's principle only limits each orbital to two electrons of opposite spin; it does not say they must spread out.

questions.s: According to the (n + l) rule, which of the following orbitals is filled first?
questions.e: n + l values: 3d = 3 + 2 = 5, 4p = 4 + 1 = 5, 4s = 4 + 0 = 4, 5s = 5 + 0 = 5. The lowest value, 4s, fills first. 3d is often chosen because its n is smaller, but the rule uses n + l, not n alone.

questions.s: Using the Rydberg equation with Rydberg constant R, the wavelength of the first line of the Lyman series of hydrogen is
questions.e: The first Lyman line is the n = 2 → n = 1 transition: 1/λ = R(1/1² − 1/2²) = 3R/4, so λ = 4/(3R). 3R/4 is the wave number 1/λ, not the wavelength.

questions.s: Which statement about cathode rays is correct?
o: They are deflected towards the negative plate
Their e/m value depends on the gas in the tube
They travel in straight lines and carry negative charge
They consist of positive ions formed from the gas in the tube
questions.e: Cathode rays are streams of electrons: they cast sharp shadows (straight-line travel) and bend towards the positive plate. Their e/m is the same whatever gas is used; it is the positive (canal) rays whose e/m depends on the gas.

questions.s: The total number of electrons with l = 1 in a ground-state iron atom (Z = 26) is
questions.e: Fe is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d⁶. l = 1 means p electrons: 2p⁶ + 3p⁶ = 12. Counting only one p subshell gives 6, and adding the six 3d electrons (which have l = 2) gives 18.

questions.s: The maximum number of electrons in an atom that can have the quantum numbers n = 4 and l = 3 is
questions.e: n = 4, l = 3 is the 4f subshell; m runs from −3 to +3, giving 7 orbitals, each holding 2 electrons of opposite spin, so 14 electrons. 7 forgets the spin quantum number, and 32 is the capacity of the whole fourth shell.

questions.s: According to VSEPR theory, the shape of the ammonia molecule, NH₃, is
questions.e: Nitrogen has three bond pairs and one lone pair; the four electron pairs point roughly tetrahedrally, but the shape is named from the atoms only, so NH₃ is trigonal pyramidal. Trigonal planar would need three bond pairs and no lone pair, as in BF₃.

questions.s: The H–C–H bond angle in methane, CH₄, is
questions.e: Carbon in CH₄ has four bond pairs and no lone pairs, arranged tetrahedrally with angles of 109.5°. 104.5° is the angle in water, where two lone pairs squeeze the bonds together.

questions.s: The hybridisation of each carbon atom in ethene, CH₂=CH₂, is
questions.e: Each carbon forms three σ bonds (two C–H, one C–C) using three sp² orbitals in a plane at 120°, and the unhybridised p orbitals overlap sideways to form the π bond. sp hybridisation is found in ethyne, which has a triple bond.

questions.s: The number of sigma (σ) and pi (π) bonds in a molecule of ethyne, H–C≡C–H, is
questions.e: The two C–H bonds are σ bonds, and the triple bond consists of one σ and two π bonds, giving 3 σ and 2 π. Every single bond, and the first bond of any multiple bond, is a σ bond, so 2 σ and 3 π reverses the count.

questions.s: Which of the following species contains a coordinate covalent bond?
questions.e: In NH₄⁺ the lone pair on nitrogen is donated to an H⁺ ion, forming a coordinate (dative) bond; once formed it is identical to the other N–H bonds. CH₄ and H₂O have only ordinary covalent bonds, and NaCl is ionic.

questions.s: Which molecule has zero dipole moment even though its individual bonds are polar?
questions.e: CCl₄ is a symmetrical tetrahedron, so the four equal C–Cl bond dipoles cancel and the net dipole moment is zero. CHCl₃ has one C–H bond in place of a C–Cl bond, so its dipoles do not cancel; NH₃ and H₂O are bent or pyramidal and are polar.

questions.s: Which bond has the greatest ionic character?
questions.e: Ionic character increases with the electronegativity difference. K (0.8) and F (4.0) differ by 3.2, larger than Na–Cl (about 2.1), Mg–O (about 2.3) and H–Cl (about 0.9). Choosing Mg–O because of the double charges confuses lattice strength with ionic character.

questions.s: The shape of the phosphorus pentachloride molecule, PCl₅, in the gas phase is
questions.e: Phosphorus has five bond pairs and no lone pairs; five pairs arrange themselves as a trigonal bipyramid (three equatorial bonds at 120°, two axial bonds at 90° to them). Octahedral needs six electron pairs, as in SF₆.

questions.s: The high electrical conductivity of metals is due to
questions.e: In a metallic bond, positive metal ions sit in a sea of delocalised valence electrons, and these electrons move freely when a voltage is applied. The positive ions are fixed in the lattice, so they do not carry the current in a solid metal.

questions.s: Bond energies: H–H = 436 kJ mol⁻¹, Cl–Cl = 243 kJ mol⁻¹, H–Cl = 432 kJ mol⁻¹. The enthalpy change for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl is
questions.e: ΔH = bonds broken − bonds formed = (436 + 243) − 2 × 432 = 679 − 864 = −185 kJ. +247 kJ forgets that two H–Cl bonds form, and +185 kJ subtracts in the wrong order.

questions.s: On the Pauling scale, the most electronegative element is
questions.e: Fluorine has the highest electronegativity, 4.0, because it is small and has a high effective nuclear charge. Oxygen (3.5) is second; chlorine has a higher electron affinity than fluorine, but that is a different property.

questions.s: In which pair do both species have the same bond angle?
questions.e: CH₄ and NH₄⁺ both have four bond pairs and no lone pairs on the central atom, so both are regular tetrahedra with 109.5° angles. BF₃ is planar (120°) but NH₃ is pyramidal (107.5°), and CO₂ and BeCl₂ are linear (180°) while H₂O is bent.

questions.s: Around the oxygen atom in a water molecule there are
o: 4 bond pairs and no lone pair
questions.e: Oxygen has six valence electrons: two are shared in the two O–H bonds and the remaining four form two lone pairs. These two lone pairs make the molecule bent with an angle of 104.5°.

questions.s: Which order of bond angles is correct?
questions.e: All three have four electron pairs, but lone pairs repel more strongly than bond pairs: CH₄ (no lone pair) 109.5°, NH₃ (one lone pair) 107.5°, H₂O (two lone pairs) 104.5°. So H₂O < NH₃ < CH₄; the first option is the exact reverse.

questions.s: Which order of carbon–carbon bond length is correct?
questions.e: More shared electron pairs pull the nuclei closer: C–C (154 pm) > C=C (134 pm) > C≡C (120 pm). Bond strength follows the opposite order, which is why the first option is a common slip.

questions.s: For an exothermic reaction at constant pressure,
o: ΔH is positive and heat is absorbed
ΔH is zero because pressure is constant
ΔH is negative and heat is released
the products have more enthalpy than the reactants
questions.e: In an exothermic reaction the products have less enthalpy than the reactants, so ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants) is negative and the difference is given out as heat. A positive ΔH with heat absorbed describes an endothermic reaction.

questions.s: The standard enthalpy of neutralisation of a strong acid by a strong base is approximately
questions.e: Strong acids and bases are fully ionised, so every such neutralisation is just H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O, releasing about 57.3 kJ per mole of water. −13.7 is the same value in kcal, and neutralisation is always exothermic, so a positive value is wrong.

questions.s: Given: C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −394 kJ mol⁻¹, and CO(g) + ½O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −283 kJ mol⁻¹. The enthalpy change for C(s) + ½O₂(g) → CO(g) is
questions.e: By Hess's law, take the first equation and subtract the second (reverse it): ΔH = −394 − (−283) = −111 kJ mol⁻¹. −677 adds the two values instead of reversing the second, and +111 has the sign error.

questions.s: In a calorimeter, Ayesha finds that a reaction raises the temperature of 100 g of water by 5.0 K. Taking the specific heat capacity of water as 4.2 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹, the heat released is
questions.e: q = mcΔT = 100 × 4.2 × 5.0 = 2100 J = 2.1 kJ. 21 kJ comes from a slip in converting joules to kilojoules; the mass must be in grams to match the units of c.

questions.s: Which equation represents the standard enthalpy of formation of water?
questions.e: Formation means one mole of the compound made from its elements in their standard states: H₂(g) and O₂(g) giving 1 mol of H₂O(l). The first equation forms 2 mol, and the third starts from gaseous atoms, which are not the standard states.

questions.s: The standard enthalpy of formation of oxygen gas, O₂(g), is
o: equal to the O=O bond energy
questions.e: By convention, every element in its standard state has a standard enthalpy of formation of zero, because forming it from itself involves no change. The O=O bond energy relates to making O atoms, not to forming O₂.

questions.s: The enthalpy of combustion of methane is −890 kJ mol⁻¹. The heat released when 8 g of methane burns completely is (C = 12, H = 1)
questions.e: Molar mass of CH₄ = 16 g mol⁻¹, so 8 g is 0.5 mol, and 0.5 × 890 = 445 kJ is released. 890 kJ treats 8 g as one mole, and 222.5 kJ uses a molar mass of 32.

questions.s: Which of the following is an endothermic process?
o: Neutralisation of HCl by NaOH solution
Reaction of sodium metal with water to give sodium hydroxide
Decomposition of calcium carbonate into CaO and CO₂
questions.e: Heating limestone is needed to break it down, because CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ absorbs about 178 kJ mol⁻¹. Combustion, neutralisation and the reaction of sodium with water all give out heat.

questions.s: In the Born–Haber cycle for sodium chloride, which step releases energy?
questions.e: Adding an electron to a chlorine atom releases energy (first electron affinity about −349 kJ mol⁻¹). Atomising sodium, ionising sodium and breaking the Cl–Cl bond all need energy, so they are endothermic.

questions.s: For NaCl: ΔHf = −411, atomisation of Na = +108, first ionisation energy of Na = +496, ½ bond energy of Cl₂ = +121 and electron affinity of Cl = −349 (all kJ mol⁻¹). The lattice energy of NaCl is
questions.e: By Hess's law, ΔHf = (108 + 496 + 121 − 349) + lattice energy, so lattice energy = −411 − 376 = −787 kJ mol⁻¹. −1485 treats the electron affinity as +349, and −35 adds 376 instead of subtracting it.

questions.s: Hess's law states that the total enthalpy change of a reaction
o: depends on the number of steps
is equal to the activation energy
is independent of the route taken
questions.e: Enthalpy is a state function, so ΔH depends only on the initial and final states, not on the path or number of steps. A catalyst changes the route and activation energy but not ΔH.

questions.s: 100 cm³ of 0.5 M H₂SO₄ is mixed with 200 cm³ of 0.5 M NaOH. Taking the enthalpy of neutralisation as −57.3 kJ per mole of water formed, the heat released is
questions.e: H₂SO₄ = 0.1 × 0.5 = 0.05 mol, giving 0.1 mol H⁺; NaOH = 0.2 × 0.5 = 0.1 mol OH⁻. So 0.1 mol of water forms and 0.1 × 57.3 = 5.73 kJ is released. 2.87 kJ forgets that sulphuric acid is diprotic.

questions.s: The pH of a 0.001 M solution of hydrochloric acid at 25 °C is
questions.e: HCl is a strong acid and ionises completely, so [H⁺] = 1 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ and pH = −log(10⁻³) = 3. 11 is the pOH of this solution, not its pH.

questions.s: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) at equilibrium, an increase in pressure shifts the equilibrium
o: towards NH₃, as the right side has fewer gas moles
towards N₂ and H₂, as pressure favours the reactants
towards NH₃, as the forward reaction is endothermic
questions.e: By Le Chatelier's principle, higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules: 4 mol on the left, 2 mol on the right, so more ammonia forms. Kp does stay constant, but the composition still changes; and the forward reaction is exothermic, not endothermic.

questions.s: The equilibrium constant expression Kc for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) is
questions.e: By the law of mass action, Kc = product concentrations over reactant concentrations, each raised to its coefficient: [NH₃]²/([N₂][H₂]³). Coefficients become powers, not multipliers, so the last option is wrong, and the third is the reverse reaction's constant.

questions.s: For which reaction is Kp equal to Kc?
questions.e: Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn, where Δn is moles of gaseous products minus gaseous reactants. For H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI, Δn = 2 − 2 = 0, so Kp = Kc. The other reactions have Δn = −2, +1 and −1.

questions.s: At equilibrium for H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), the concentrations are [H₂] = 0.1, [I₂] = 0.1 and [HI] = 0.8 mol dm⁻³. The value of Kc is
questions.e: Kc = [HI]²/([H₂][I₂]) = 0.64/(0.1 × 0.1) = 0.64/0.01 = 64. 80 forgets to square [HI], and 8 also ignores the square while using only one reactant.

questions.s: The pH of a 0.01 M solution of sodium hydroxide at 25 °C is (Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴)
questions.e: NaOH is fully ionised, so [OH⁻] = 10⁻² and pOH = 2. Since pH + pOH = 14 at 25 °C, pH = 12. 2 is the pOH, which is the most common slip.

questions.s: Which of the following mixtures acts as a buffer solution?
questions.e: A buffer contains a weak acid and its salt with a strong base (or a weak base and its salt): ethanoic acid with sodium ethanoate resists changes in pH. HCl and HNO₃ are strong acids, and NaOH is a strong base, so their mixtures with salts cannot buffer.

questions.s: The solubility of silver chloride in water at 25 °C is 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³. Its solubility product, Ksp, is
questions.e: AgCl ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻, so [Ag⁺] = [Cl⁻] = s and Ksp = s² = (1.0 × 10⁻⁵)² = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰. 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ adds the two ion concentrations instead of multiplying them.

questions.s: The solubility of calcium fluoride, CaF₂, in water is 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³. Its solubility product is
questions.e: CaF₂ ⇌ Ca²⁺ + 2F⁻, so [Ca²⁺] = s and [F⁻] = 2s; Ksp = s(2s)² = 4s³ = 4 × 8.0 × 10⁻¹² = 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹. 8.0 × 10⁻¹² is s³, which forgets that [F⁻] is 2s.

questions.s: When solid sodium chloride is added to a saturated solution of silver chloride, the solubility of AgCl
o: increases, as more ions are present
decreases, as Cl⁻ is a common ion
stays the same, as Ksp is constant
decreases, as the Ksp of AgCl falls
questions.e: Extra Cl⁻ makes the ionic product [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] exceed Ksp, so AgCl precipitates and less of it can dissolve: the common ion effect. Ksp itself does not change at constant temperature; only the solubility falls.

questions.s: A catalyst increases the rate of a reversible reaction because it
o: shifts the equilibrium towards the products
makes ΔH of the reaction more negative
questions.e: A catalyst provides an alternative path with a lower activation energy, speeding up both forward and reverse reactions equally. It therefore does not change ΔH, Kc or the position of equilibrium; it only helps equilibrium to be reached sooner.

questions.s: A reactant decomposes by a first-order reaction with a half-life of 10 minutes. Starting with 80 g of it, the mass remaining after 30 minutes is
questions.e: 30 minutes is three half-lives: 80 → 40 → 20 → 10 g. 26.7 g divides 80 by 3, treating the decay as linear, and 20 g stops after two half-lives.

questions.s: The rate law of a reaction is rate = k[A]²[B]. If the concentration of A is doubled and that of B is also doubled, the rate becomes
questions.e: New rate = k(2[A])²(2[B]) = 4 × 2 × k[A]²[B] = 8 times the original. 4 times considers only the change in A, and 6 times adds the factors instead of multiplying them.

questions.s: For a second-order reaction with concentrations in mol dm⁻³ and time in seconds, the unit of the rate constant k is
questions.e: Rate = k[A]², so k = rate/[A]² = (mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹)/(mol dm⁻³)² = dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹. s⁻¹ is the unit for a first-order reaction, and mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹ belongs to a third-order reaction.

questions.s: At 25 °C, the hydroxide ion concentration in a solution of pH 4 is (Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴)
questions.e: [H⁺] = 10⁻⁴, and [H⁺][OH⁻] = 10⁻¹⁴, so [OH⁻] = 10⁻¹⁴/10⁻⁴ = 10⁻¹⁰ mol dm⁻³. 1 × 10⁻⁴ is the hydrogen ion concentration, and 1 × 10⁻⁷ applies only to a neutral solution.

questions.s: For an exothermic reaction at equilibrium, increasing the temperature
o: increases Kc and the yield of products
has no effect on the value of Kc
decreases Kc and the yield of products
increases only the rate of the forward reaction
questions.e: Raising the temperature favours the endothermic direction, which here is the reverse reaction, so the equilibrium shifts left and Kc decreases. Temperature is the only factor that changes Kc, and it speeds up both forward and reverse reactions.

questions.s: The rate of a certain reaction doubles for every 10 °C rise in temperature. Compared with its rate at 30 °C, its rate at 70 °C is
questions.e: A rise of 40 °C is four 10 °C steps, so the rate increases by 2⁴ = 16 times. 4 times counts the steps instead of using them as powers, and 8 times uses only three steps.

questions.s: 1.0 mol of PCl₅ is heated in a closed 1.0 dm³ vessel: PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g). At equilibrium 50 % of the PCl₅ has dissociated. The value of Kc is
questions.e: At equilibrium [PCl₅] = 0.5, [PCl₃] = 0.5 and [Cl₂] = 0.5 mol dm⁻³, so Kc = (0.5 × 0.5)/0.5 = 0.50. 0.25 uses the initial 1.0 mol dm⁻³ for PCl₅ instead of the equilibrium value.

questions.s: The oxidation number of chromium in potassium dichromate, K₂Cr₂O₇, is
questions.e: 2(+1) + 2x + 7(−2) = 0 gives 2x = 12, so x = +6. +12 is the total for both chromium atoms, and +3 is chromium's oxidation number after dichromate has been reduced.

questions.s: 4.0 g of sodium hydroxide is dissolved in water and the solution is made up to 250 cm³. Its molarity is (Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1)
questions.e: Moles of NaOH = 4.0/40 = 0.1 mol, and volume = 0.250 dm³, so M = 0.1/0.250 = 0.4 M. 0.1 M forgets that the volume is only a quarter of a litre, and 0.016 M divides grams by cm³.

questions.s: 9.0 g of glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆, molar mass 180 g mol⁻¹) is dissolved in 250 g of water. The molality of the solution is
questions.e: Moles of glucose = 9.0/180 = 0.05 mol, and mass of solvent = 0.250 kg, so molality = 0.05/0.250 = 0.2 mol kg⁻¹. 0.05 m is just the number of moles, which ignores the mass of water.

questions.s: The vapour pressure of a pure solvent is 30 torr. A non-volatile solute is dissolved so that the mole fraction of the solvent is 0.9. By Raoult's law, the vapour pressure of the solution is
questions.e: Raoult's law: p = x(solvent) × p° = 0.9 × 30 = 27 torr. 3 torr is the lowering of vapour pressure, not the vapour pressure itself, and a non-volatile solute can never raise it to 33 torr.

questions.s: Colligative properties of a dilute solution depend mainly on
o: the chemical nature of the solute
the molar mass of the solvent alone
questions.e: Colligative properties (vapour-pressure lowering, boiling-point elevation, freezing-point depression, osmotic pressure) depend on how many solute particles are present, not on what they are. That is why 0.1 m NaCl has about twice the effect of 0.1 m glucose.

questions.s: 0.5 mol of sodium chloride is dissolved in 1 kg of water. Assuming complete dissociation and Kb (water) = 0.52 K kg mol⁻¹, the boiling point of the solution is
questions.e: NaCl gives two ions, so the particle molality is 2 × 0.5 = 1.0 m and ΔTb = 0.52 × 1.0 = 0.52 K, giving 100.52 °C. 100.26 °C ignores dissociation, and 99.48 °C wrongly lowers the boiling point.

questions.s: Which aqueous solution has the lowest freezing point?
questions.e: Freezing-point depression is proportional to the molality of particles: CaCl₂ gives 3 ions (0.3 m), NaCl gives 2 (0.2 m), while glucose and urea do not ionise (0.1 m). The largest depression means the lowest freezing point, so CaCl₂.

questions.s: During the electrolysis of molten sodium chloride, the product formed at the cathode is
questions.e: The cathode is where reduction happens: Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na. Chlorine forms at the anode by oxidation of Cl⁻. Hydrogen appears only when water is present, as in the electrolysis of brine.

questions.s: A charge of 0.2 faraday is passed through copper(II) sulphate solution. The mass of copper deposited at the cathode is (Cu = 63.5)
questions.e: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, so 2 F deposit 1 mol of Cu; 0.2 F deposit 0.1 mol = 6.35 g. 12.7 g assumes one faraday per mole of copper, ignoring the 2+ charge.

questions.s: Standard electrode potentials: Zn²⁺/Zn = −0.76 V and Cu²⁺/Cu = +0.34 V. The standard emf of the Daniell cell, Zn | Zn²⁺ || Cu²⁺ | Cu, is
questions.e: E°cell = E°(cathode) − E°(anode) = 0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V, with copper as the cathode. 0.42 V comes from ignoring the negative sign of the zinc potential, and a working galvanic cell has a positive emf.

questions.s: In a galvanic (voltaic) cell, oxidation takes place at the
questions.e: Oxidation always occurs at the anode; in a galvanic cell the anode releases electrons into the external circuit, so it is the negative electrode. In electrolysis the anode is positive, which is why the third option is a common confusion.

questions.s: In acidic solution, MnO₄⁻ oxidises Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ and is itself reduced to Mn²⁺. The number of moles of Fe²⁺ oxidised by one mole of MnO₄⁻ is
questions.e: Manganese goes from +7 to +2, gaining 5 electrons, while each Fe²⁺ loses only 1 electron, so one MnO₄⁻ oxidises 5 Fe²⁺: MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O. Choosing 1 ignores electron balance.

questions.s: Standard reduction potentials: Li⁺/Li = −3.04 V, Zn²⁺/Zn = −0.76 V, Cu²⁺/Cu = +0.34 V, Ag⁺/Ag = +0.80 V. The strongest reducing agent among these metals is
questions.e: The most negative reduction potential means the metal gives up electrons most readily, so lithium is the strongest reducing agent. Silver has the most positive potential, so Ag⁺ is the strongest oxidising agent, and Ag is the weakest reducing agent.

questions.s: Galvanised iron (iron coated with zinc) does not rust even when the coating is scratched, because
o: zinc is less reactive than iron and never corrodes
zinc is oxidised in preference to iron
zinc reduces the rust back to iron metal
zinc stops oxygen from dissolving in water
questions.e: Zinc has a more negative electrode potential than iron, so it acts as the anode and is oxidised instead of iron (sacrificial protection). Zinc is more reactive than iron, not less; tin plating, by contrast, protects only while unbroken.

questions.s: During the discharge of a lead–acid accumulator,
o: the sulphuric acid becomes more concentrated and denser
lead dioxide is formed on both of the electrodes
lead at the negative plate is reduced to lead sulphate
lead sulphate forms on both plates and the acid gets diluted
questions.e: On discharge, Pb is oxidised to PbSO₄ at the negative plate and PbO₂ is reduced to PbSO₄ at the positive plate; both reactions use up H₂SO₄ and produce water, so the acid's density falls. Lead going to Pb²⁺ is oxidation, not reduction.

questions.s: The oxidation number of sulphur in the thiosulphate ion, S₂O₃²⁻, is
questions.e: 2x + 3(−2) = −2 gives 2x = +4, so the average oxidation number is +2. +2.5 is the value in the tetrathionate ion S₄O₆²⁻, and +6 is the value in sulphate.

questions.s: A current of 5.0 A is passed through silver nitrate solution. The time needed to deposit 1.08 g of silver is (Ag = 108; F = 96500 C mol⁻¹)
questions.e: 1.08 g = 0.01 mol Ag, and Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag needs 0.01 F = 965 C. Time = Q/I = 965/5.0 = 193 s. 965 s is the charge in coulombs mistaken for time.

questions.s: A solution is made by mixing 36 g of water with 46 g of ethanol, C₂H₅OH. The mole fraction of water in the solution is (H = 1, C = 12, O = 16)
questions.e: Water = 36/18 = 2 mol and ethanol = 46/46 = 1 mol, so x(water) = 2/(2 + 1) = 0.67. 0.44 is the mass fraction 36/82, and 0.33 is the mole fraction of ethanol.

questions.s: Across a period from left to right, the atomic radius generally
o: increases, as more electrons are added
stays constant, as the shell is the same
questions.e: Across a period electrons enter the same shell while the nuclear charge rises by one each step; shielding from same-shell electrons is poor, so the outer electrons are pulled closer and the radius falls. Adding electrons does not enlarge the atom because no new shell is started.

questions.s: Which of the following elements has the highest first ionisation energy?
questions.e: Helium's two electrons are in the 1s orbital, very close to the nucleus with no shielding, so it has the highest first ionisation energy of all elements (about 2372 kJ mol⁻¹). Neon is next among these, but its electrons are in the second shell, further from the nucleus.

questions.s: The first ionisation energy of nitrogen is higher than that of oxygen because
o: nitrogen has a stable half-filled 2p subshell
nitrogen has the larger nuclear charge
oxygen has the smaller atomic radius
oxygen has fewer electrons in total
questions.e: Nitrogen's 2p³ has one electron in each orbital, a stable half-filled arrangement; in oxygen (2p⁴) one orbital holds a pair, and repulsion between the paired electrons makes one easier to remove. Oxygen actually has the larger nuclear charge (8 versus 7), so that cannot be the reason.

questions.s: Which element has the highest (most exothermic) first electron affinity?
questions.e: Chlorine releases about 349 kJ mol⁻¹, slightly more than fluorine (about 328 kJ mol⁻¹). Fluorine's very small 2p shell is crowded, so the incoming electron feels strong repulsion; this is why the expected answer F is wrong.

questions.s: Sodium metal is stored under kerosene oil because it
o: reacts readily with air and moisture
is a poor conductor of heat
questions.e: Sodium is very reactive: it tarnishes quickly in air and reacts vigorously with water, so it is kept under kerosene, with which it does not react. It does not dissolve in kerosene; the oil simply keeps air and moisture away.

questions.s: Which alkali metal carbonate decomposes on ordinary strong heating to give carbon dioxide?
questions.e: The small Li⁺ ion has a high polarising power and distorts the carbonate ion, so Li₂CO₃ → Li₂O + CO₂ on heating, just like MgCO₃ (diagonal relationship). The larger Na⁺, K⁺ and Rb⁺ ions polarise carbonate weakly, so their carbonates are stable to heat.

questions.s: Which of the following hydroxides is the most soluble in water?
questions.e: The solubility of group II hydroxides increases down the group, because lattice energy falls faster than hydration energy as the cation gets bigger; Ba(OH)₂ is the most soluble. Mg(OH)₂ is only sparingly soluble, which is why it is used as milk of magnesia.

questions.s: Plaster of Paris, used for setting broken bones, has the formula
questions.e: Heating gypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O) to about 120 °C drives off part of the water, giving (CaSO₄)₂·H₂O, plaster of Paris; when mixed with water it sets back into gypsum. CaSO₄·2H₂O is gypsum itself, and CaCO₃·MgCO₃ is dolomite.

questions.s: The chemical formula of borax is
questions.e: Borax is sodium tetraborate decahydrate, Na₂B₄O₇·10H₂O, the main source of boron compounds. H₃BO₃ is boric acid, Na₂CO₃·10H₂O is washing soda, and Al₂O₃·2H₂O is bauxite.

questions.s: Which of the following oxides is amphoteric?
questions.e: Al₂O₃ reacts with acids (giving Al³⁺ salts) and with alkalis (giving aluminates), so it is amphoteric. Na₂O and MgO are basic oxides, and SO₃ is an acidic oxide.

questions.s: Lead commonly shows the +2 oxidation state rather than +4 in its compounds. This is due to
questions.e: Down group IV the 6s² pair of lead becomes reluctant to take part in bonding (the inert pair effect), so Pb²⁺ is more stable than Pb⁴⁺. Lead is a large atom and does have filled d and f subshells, so the first two options are false.

questions.s: Copper reacts with concentrated nitric acid. The main gaseous product is
questions.e: Cu + 4HNO₃(conc) → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO₂ + 2H₂O, giving brown fumes of NO₂. Dilute nitric acid gives NO instead, and nitric acid does not release hydrogen with copper because nitrate is reduced rather than H⁺.

questions.s: Which of the following reactions takes place in aqueous solution?
questions.e: Oxidising power of the halogens falls down the group (F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂), so a halogen displaces only those below it. Chlorine therefore oxidises bromide to bromine; bromine and iodine cannot oxidise chloride.

questions.s: The noble gas that forms the largest number of stable compounds, such as fluorides and oxides, is
questions.e: Xenon is large and has the lowest ionisation energy of these, so it forms compounds such as XeF₂, XeF₄, XeF₆ and XeO₃. No stable compounds of helium or neon are known, because their electrons are held very tightly.

questions.s: In water, hydrofluoric acid is a much weaker acid than hydrochloric acid. The main reason is that
o: fluorine is the least electronegative halogen
the H–F bond is very strong
HF does not dissolve in water
HF is a gas at room temperature
questions.e: The H–F bond is short and very strong (about 568 kJ mol⁻¹), so HF releases H⁺ to water only slightly. Fluorine is the most electronegative halogen, not the least, and HF is in fact very soluble in water.

questions.s: Lithium shows a diagonal relationship, resembling in many properties the element
questions.e: Li and Mg have similar polarising power (charge-to-size ratio), so both form nitrides on burning, have carbonates that decompose on heating and have only slightly soluble fluorides. Beryllium sits diagonally to aluminium, not to lithium.

questions.s: The first four ionisation energies of an element are 738, 1451, 7733 and 10540 kJ mol⁻¹. The element most likely belongs to
questions.e: The big jump comes between the second (1451) and third (7733) ionisation energies, so the atom has two outer electrons before an inner shell is reached: a group 2 element (this is magnesium). A group 1 element would show the jump after the first ionisation energy.

questions.s: Chlorine reacts with hot concentrated sodium hydroxide to give NaCl, NaClO₃ and water. The oxidation state of chlorine in NaClO₃, and the type of reaction, are
questions.e: In NaClO₃: +1 + x + 3(−2) = 0, so x = +5. Chlorine (0) is both reduced to Cl⁻ (−1) and oxidised to ClO₃⁻ (+5), which is disproportionation: 3Cl₂ + 6NaOH → 5NaCl + NaClO₃ + 3H₂O. +1 is the value in NaOCl, formed with cold dilute alkali.

questions.s: The ground-state electronic configuration of copper (Z = 29) is
questions.e: A completely filled 3d¹⁰ subshell is extra stable, so one 4s electron moves into 3d, giving [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹. [Ar] 3d⁹ 4s² is what simple Aufbau filling predicts, and [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² has 30 electrons, which is zinc.

questions.s: Most compounds of transition elements are coloured. This is mainly due to
o: electron transitions between split d orbitals
complete filling of the outer s orbital
emission of particles from the nucleus
their high melting and boiling points
questions.e: Ligands split the d orbitals into two energy levels; an electron in a partly filled d subshell absorbs visible light to jump between them, and the complementary colour is seen. Ions with d⁰ or d¹⁰ configurations cannot do this and are colourless.

questions.s: Which of the following ions is colourless in aqueous solution?
questions.e: Zn²⁺ is 3d¹⁰: its d subshell is full, so no d–d transition is possible and its salts are colourless. Cu²⁺ (d⁹) is blue, Cr³⁺ (d³) is green or violet, and Fe³⁺ (d⁵) gives yellow-brown solutions.

questions.s: The number of unpaired electrons in the Fe³⁺ ion (Z of Fe = 26) is
questions.e: Fe is [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s²; it loses both 4s electrons and one 3d electron to form Fe³⁺, [Ar] 3d⁵. By Hund's rule each of the five d orbitals holds one electron, so there are 5 unpaired electrons. 6 is the number of d electrons in the neutral atom, which has 4 unpaired.

questions.s: In potassium ferrocyanide, K₄[Fe(CN)₆], the oxidation state and the coordination number of iron are
questions.e: The complex ion carries 4− (balanced by 4 K⁺); six CN⁻ give −6, so Fe + (−6) = −4 and Fe = +2. Six ligands are attached, so the coordination number is 6. +3 belongs to K₃[Fe(CN)₆], and 4 is the number of K⁺ ions, not ligands.

questions.s: Which of the following is a bidentate ligand?
questions.e: Ethylenediamine, H₂N–CH₂–CH₂–NH₂, has two nitrogen atoms, each with a lone pair, so it binds a metal ion at two points and forms a ring (chelate). NH₃, CN⁻ and H₂O each donate through only one atom, so they are monodentate.

questions.s: When sodium hydroxide is added to an orange solution of potassium dichromate, the solution turns yellow because
o: chromium is oxidised to the +7 state
Cr₂O₇²⁻ forms a green complex with OH⁻
questions.e: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 2OH⁻ ⇌ 2CrO₄²⁻ + H₂O: in alkali the orange dichromate changes into yellow chromate. Chromium stays at +6 in both ions, so this is not a redox change; Cr³⁺ would be green.

questions.s: When potassium permanganate acts as an oxidising agent in acidic medium, the oxidation state of manganese changes from
questions.e: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O, so Mn goes from +7 to +2 and the purple colour disappears. +7 to +4 (forming brown MnO₂) happens in neutral or weakly alkaline solution.

questions.s: Which form of iron contains the least carbon?
questions.e: Wrought iron is the purest commercial iron, with only about 0.1–0.25 % carbon, which makes it soft and malleable. Pig iron and cast iron contain roughly 2.5–4.5 % carbon, and steels lie in between.

questions.s: Using μ = √(n(n + 2)) BM, where n is the number of unpaired electrons, the spin-only magnetic moment of the Cr³⁺ ion (Z of Cr = 24) is
questions.e: Cr is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹; Cr³⁺ is [Ar] 3d³ with 3 unpaired electrons, so μ = √(3 × 5) = √15 ≈ 3.87 BM. √24 uses n = 4, which forgets that the 4s electron leaves first along with two 3d electrons.

questions.s: Which element is not regarded as a typical transition element, because its d subshell is completely filled both in the atom and in its common ion?
questions.e: Zinc is 3d¹⁰ 4s² and Zn²⁺ is 3d¹⁰, so it never has a partly filled d subshell. Copper atom is 3d¹⁰ 4s¹, but Cu²⁺ is 3d⁹, so copper counts as a transition element.

questions.s: The IUPAC name of [Cu(NH₃)₄]SO₄ is
questions.e: The complex cation is named first, ligands before the metal: four NH₃ = tetraammine; sulphate is 2−, so copper is +2, giving tetraamminecopper(II) sulphate. The ending -ate (cuprate) is used only when the complex is an anion.

questions.s: Which of the following compounds is a ketone?
questions.e: In a ketone the carbonyl group C=O is bonded to two carbon atoms, as in propanone, CH₃COCH₃. CH₃CHO has the carbonyl at the end of the chain with a hydrogen attached, so it is an aldehyde; the others are an alcohol and a carboxylic acid.

questions.s: The general formula of the alkynes is
questions.e: A triple bond removes four hydrogens compared with the alkane CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, giving CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ (for example C₂H₂). CₙH₂ₙ is the formula of alkenes and cycloalkanes, and CₙH₂ₙ₊₁ is an alkyl group, not a compound.

questions.s: The number of structural isomers with the molecular formula C₅H₁₂ is
questions.e: C₅H₁₂ has three chain isomers: pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane. Names such as 3-methylbutane or 2-ethylpropane describe one of these same molecules, so counting them gives a false 4 or 5.

questions.s: The IUPAC name of CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–CH₃ is
questions.e: The longest chain has four carbons (butane), with a methyl branch; numbering from the end nearer the branch puts it on carbon 2, giving 2-methylbutane. 3-methylbutane numbers from the wrong end, and the compound is not pentane because its chain is branched.

questions.s: Which of the following alkenes shows geometrical (cis–trans) isomerism?
questions.e: Cis–trans isomerism needs two different groups on each carbon of the C=C bond. In but-2-ene, CH₃CH=CHCH₃, each double-bond carbon carries H and CH₃. Propene, but-1-ene and 2-methylpropene all have one double-bond carbon with two identical groups.

questions.s: Propene reacts with hydrogen bromide in the absence of peroxides. The main product is
questions.e: By Markovnikov's rule, H adds to the double-bond carbon that already has more hydrogens, because the more stable secondary carbocation forms; Br then attaches to the middle carbon, giving CH₃CHBrCH₃. 1-bromopropane is the anti-Markovnikov product formed only with peroxides.

questions.s: Which compound rapidly decolourises bromine water at room temperature, without sunlight?
questions.e: Ethene has a C=C bond that undergoes electrophilic addition with bromine, forming colourless 1,2-dibromoethane. Alkanes react with bromine only in light by substitution, and benzene resists addition because of its delocalised π system.

questions.s: The reaction of methane with chlorine in diffused sunlight takes place by
questions.e: Light splits Cl₂ into chlorine free radicals, which remove hydrogen from methane in a chain reaction, replacing H by Cl. Methane has no π bond, so addition is impossible, and no electrophile or nucleophile is involved.

questions.s: In the laboratory, ethyne is prepared by the action of water on
questions.e: CaC₂ + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + C₂H₂. Aluminium carbide with water gives methane, and heating sodium ethanoate with soda lime also gives methane, so those are the tempting wrong choices.

questions.s: In the nitration of benzene with a mixture of concentrated nitric and sulphuric acids, the electrophile that attacks the ring is
questions.e: Sulphuric acid protonates nitric acid, which loses water to give the nitronium ion: HNO₃ + 2H₂SO₄ → NO₂⁺ + H₃O⁺ + 2HSO₄⁻. An electrophile must be electron-seeking, so the negatively charged NO₂⁻ and NO₃⁻ cannot play that role.

questions.s: Ethene is shaken with cold, dilute alkaline potassium permanganate (Baeyer's reagent). The organic product is
questions.e: Cold dilute KMnO₄ adds two OH groups across the double bond, giving HOCH₂CH₂OH (ethylene glycol), and the purple colour fades. Hot concentrated permanganate would break the molecule further; ethanol forms only by adding water, not by oxidation.

questions.s: Benzene usually undergoes substitution rather than addition reactions because
o: it has no π electrons at all in its ring
it is a saturated cyclic hydrocarbon
its carbon–hydrogen bonds are unusually weak
addition would destroy its delocalised π system
questions.e: The six π electrons of benzene are delocalised over the ring, giving extra stability (resonance energy). Substitution keeps this aromatic system, whereas addition would destroy it. Benzene is unsaturated and does have π electrons, so the first two options are false.

questions.s: All carbon–carbon bonds in benzene have the same length, about 139 pm. This length is
o: shorter than a C=C double bond
between C–C and C=C bond lengths
longer than a C–C single bond
equal to a C≡C triple bond length
questions.e: Each ring bond has a bond order of 1.5 because the π electrons are delocalised, so its length (139 pm) lies between C–C (154 pm) and C=C (134 pm). The Kekulé picture of alternating single and double bonds would predict two different lengths.

questions.s: In the Friedel–Crafts methylation of benzene with chloromethane, the role of anhydrous aluminium chloride is to
questions.e: AlCl₃ is a Lewis acid: CH₃Cl + AlCl₃ → CH₃⁺ + AlCl₄⁻. The methyl cation then attacks the ring, and H⁺ is lost to give methylbenzene (toluene). AlCl₃ accepts an electron pair, so it is not a nucleophile; no water is formed in this reaction.

questions.s: Nitrobenzene is nitrated further with a mixture of concentrated nitric and sulphuric acids. The main product is
questions.e: The –NO₂ group withdraws electrons from the ring, deactivating especially the ortho and para positions, so the second nitro group enters the meta position. Ortho and para products dominate only with electron-donating groups such as –CH₃ or –OH.

questions.s: Alkanes are also called paraffins because they
questions.e: Paraffin means little affinity: alkanes have only strong, non-polar C–C and C–H σ bonds, so they react with few reagents. They do not decolourise bromine water in the dark, contain only single bonds and are insoluble in water.

questions.s: Which reagent distinguishes ethyne from ethene?
questions.e: Ethyne has acidic hydrogens on its sp-hybridised carbons and gives a white precipitate of silver acetylide with ammoniacal AgNO₃; ethene does not react. Bromine water, permanganate and hydrogen react with both unsaturated compounds, so they cannot tell them apart.

questions.s: The number of σ and π bonds in a molecule of propene, CH₂=CH–CH₃, is
questions.e: Propene has 6 C–H bonds and 2 C–C bonds, all containing one σ bond each, so 8 σ; the double bond adds 1 π bond. Counting the double bond as two π bonds, or forgetting the σ part of it, gives the wrong combinations.

questions.s: Ethene is passed with hydrogen over finely divided nickel at about 200–300 °C. The product is
questions.e: This is catalytic hydrogenation: CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ → CH₃CH₃. Adding hydrogen removes the double bond, so it cannot give ethyne, which has fewer hydrogens, and no oxygen is present to form ethanol.

questions.s: A concentrated aqueous solution of sodium ethanoate is electrolysed (Kolbe's method). The hydrocarbon formed at the anode is
questions.e: At the anode, 2CH₃COO⁻ → 2CH₃• + 2CO₂ + 2e⁻, and two methyl radicals join to form CH₃–CH₃. Methane is the product of heating sodium ethanoate with soda lime, a different reaction.

questions.s: Which statement about an SN2 reaction is correct?
o: It proceeds through a carbocation intermediate
Its rate depends only on the alkyl halide concentration
It occurs in one step with inversion of configuration
It is fastest for tertiary alkyl halides
questions.e: In SN2 the nucleophile attacks from the side opposite the leaving group while the C–X bond breaks, in a single step, so the configuration is inverted. The carbocation, first-order rate law and preference for tertiary halides all describe SN1.

questions.s: With Lucas reagent (concentrated HCl and anhydrous ZnCl₂), which alcohol turns cloudy immediately at room temperature?
questions.e: Tertiary alcohols form a stable tertiary carbocation and give the insoluble alkyl chloride at once. 2-methylpropan-2-ol is tertiary; propan-2-ol (secondary) takes about five minutes, and primary alcohols such as ethanol hardly react at room temperature.

questions.s: Methylmagnesium bromide, CH₃MgBr, reacts with methanal (HCHO) and the product is then hydrolysed with dilute acid. The alcohol formed is
questions.e: The CH₃ group of the Grignard reagent adds to the carbonyl carbon of HCHO, and hydrolysis gives CH₃–CH₂OH, a primary alcohol with one more carbon. Methanal always gives primary alcohols; propan-2-ol would come from ethanal, and 2-methylpropan-2-ol from propanone.

questions.s: Phenol is a stronger acid than ethanol because
o: ethanol molecules contain a benzene ring
only phenol can form hydrogen bonds
the phenoxide ion is stabilised by resonance
questions.e: After losing H⁺, the negative charge on the phenoxide ion is delocalised into the benzene ring, which stabilises the ion and favours ionisation. The ethoxide ion has no such delocalisation. Both phenol and ethanol form hydrogen bonds, so that cannot explain the difference.

questions.s: Williamson's synthesis of diethyl ether uses
questions.e: C₂H₅O⁻Na⁺ + C₂H₅Br → C₂H₅–O–C₂H₅ + NaBr, an SN2 reaction of the alkoxide with an alkyl halide. Ethanol with sulphuric acid at 180 °C gives ethene, and steam with ethene gives ethanol.

questions.s: Bromoethane is heated with alcoholic potassium hydroxide. The main organic product is
questions.e: In alcohol, OH⁻ acts mainly as a base and removes H⁺ from the carbon next to C–Br, eliminating HBr to give CH₂=CH₂. Aqueous KOH favours substitution, which would give ethanol instead.

questions.s: Which alkyl halide reacts fastest by the SN1 mechanism?
questions.e: The slow step of SN1 is formation of a carbocation, so the most stable carbocation reacts fastest: the tertiary (CH₃)₃C⁺, stabilised by three alkyl groups. (CH₃)₂CHCH₂Br is branched but still a primary halide, so it reacts slowly by SN1.

questions.s: Which of the following is a secondary alcohol?
questions.e: In butan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃, the carbon carrying –OH is bonded to two other carbons, which makes it secondary. 2-methylpropan-2-ol is tertiary, and the two -1-ol compounds are primary.

questions.s: Propan-2-ol is warmed with acidified potassium dichromate. The organic product is
questions.e: Secondary alcohols are oxidised to ketones: CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ → CH₃COCH₃, and the orange dichromate turns green. Propanal and propanoic acid come from oxidising propan-1-ol, a primary alcohol.

questions.s: Phenol reacts with bromine water at room temperature to give a white precipitate of
questions.e: The –OH group strongly activates the ortho and para positions, so all three (2, 4 and 6) are substituted at once, without a catalyst. Monobromophenols are obtained only with bromine in a non-polar solvent such as CS₂ at low temperature.

questions.s: Methylmagnesium iodide reacts with propanone, and the product is hydrolysed with dilute acid. The alcohol obtained is
questions.e: CH₃⁻ from the Grignard reagent adds to the carbonyl carbon of (CH₃)₂C=O, and hydrolysis gives (CH₃)₃C–OH, a tertiary alcohol. Ketones always give tertiary alcohols with Grignard reagents; butan-2-ol would come from ethanal with C₂H₅MgX.

questions.s: Ethanol is heated with excess concentrated sulphuric acid at about 170 °C. The main organic product is
questions.e: At about 170 °C with excess acid, ethanol is dehydrated: C₂H₅OH → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O. Diethyl ether forms at a lower temperature (about 140 °C) with excess ethanol, and ethyl hydrogen sulphate is only an intermediate.

questions.s: For a given alkyl group, the correct order of reactivity of alkyl halides in nucleophilic substitution is
questions.e: The C–X bond gets longer and weaker from C–F to C–I, so iodide leaves most easily and alkyl iodides react fastest. Choosing fluorides first follows bond polarity, but bond strength matters more here.

questions.s: Ethylmagnesium bromide, C₂H₅MgBr, reacts with water. The organic product is
questions.e: The ethyl group of a Grignard reagent behaves as a carbanion and takes H⁺ from water: C₂H₅MgBr + H₂O → C₂H₆ + Mg(OH)Br. Ethanol is not formed because no new C–O bond is made; that is why Grignard reagents must be kept dry.

questions.s: Which reagent gives a violet colour with phenol but not with ethanol?
questions.e: Phenol forms a violet complex with neutral iron(III) chloride, a standard test for phenols. Sodium reacts with both, releasing hydrogen without any colour, and Tollens' reagent tests for aldehydes.

questions.s: Diethyl ether is heated with excess concentrated hydroiodic acid. The organic product is
questions.e: HI cleaves the C–O–C linkage: C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + HI → C₂H₅I + C₂H₅OH, and with excess HI the ethanol is also converted, so the overall product is 2C₂H₅I + H₂O. Ethanol only appears when the acid is not in excess, and it is then accompanied by iodoethane.

questions.s: The correct order of acid strength is
questions.e: Phenol (Ka about 10⁻¹⁰) ionises more than water because phenoxide is resonance stabilised, and ethanol is weaker than water because the ethyl group pushes electrons onto oxygen, destabilising ethoxide. So phenol > water > ethanol; this is why sodium ethoxide is a stronger base than NaOH.

questions.s: The hydrolysis of bromomethane by hydroxide ions follows the SN2 mechanism. If the concentration of CH₃Br is doubled and the concentration of OH⁻ is also doubled, the rate increases
questions.e: SN2 is bimolecular: rate = k[CH₃Br][OH⁻], so doubling each gives 2 × 2 = 4 times the rate. 2 times would apply to SN1, whose rate depends only on the alkyl halide.

questions.s: Which compound gives a silver mirror when warmed with Tollens' reagent?
questions.e: Aldehydes are easily oxidised, so ethanal reduces Ag⁺ in ammoniacal silver nitrate to metallic silver, which coats the tube as a mirror. Ketones such as propanone are not oxidised by this mild reagent, so they give no mirror.

questions.s: Which compound gives a yellow precipitate of iodoform when warmed with iodine and sodium hydroxide?
questions.e: The iodoform test is positive for compounds containing CH₃CO– (or CH₃CH(OH)–, which is oxidised to it). Propanone, CH₃COCH₃, has this group and gives CHI₃. Propanal, CH₃CH₂CHO, has its carbonyl attached to an ethyl group, so it does not react.

questions.s: Ethanal reacts with hydrogen cyanide in the presence of a little base. The product is
questions.e: CN⁻ attacks the carbonyl carbon (nucleophilic addition) and the oxygen then takes H⁺, giving the cyanohydrin CH₃CH(OH)CN, 2-hydroxypropanenitrile. The CN carbon becomes part of the chain, so the name is based on propane, not ethane.

questions.s: When ethanal is warmed with Fehling's solution, a red precipitate forms. The precipitate is
questions.e: The aldehyde reduces the blue Cu²⁺ complex to copper(I) oxide, Cu₂O, which is brick red, while the aldehyde is oxidised to the carboxylate ion. CuO is black, and Cu(OH)₂ is the pale blue copper(II) compound.

questions.s: Propanone is reduced with sodium borohydride, NaBH₄. The product is
questions.e: Reduction adds hydrogen across C=O, so the ketone CH₃COCH₃ gives the secondary alcohol CH₃CH(OH)CH₃. Propan-1-ol would come from reducing the aldehyde propanal, and NaBH₄ does not reduce a carbonyl group all the way to an alkane.

questions.s: Ethanoic acid is heated with ethanol and a few drops of concentrated sulphuric acid. The fruity-smelling product is
questions.e: Esterification: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O. The ester is named alkyl (from the alcohol) then -oate (from the acid): ethyl ethanoate. Ethyl methanoate would need methanoic acid.

questions.s: Which of the following is the strongest acid?
questions.e: Chlorine atoms withdraw electrons by the inductive effect, spreading the negative charge of the carboxylate ion and stabilising it; three chlorines do this most, so trichloroethanoic acid is strongest. Ethanoic acid, with no chlorine, is the weakest of the four.

questions.s: Ethanoic acid gives effervescence of carbon dioxide, but phenol does not, with
questions.e: Carboxylic acids are stronger than carbonic acid, so they release CO₂ from NaHCO₃; phenol is weaker than carbonic acid and cannot. Sodium metal reacts with both, giving hydrogen, not CO₂, and NaOH neutralises both without any gas.

questions.s: Ammonium ethanoate is heated strongly. The organic product is
questions.e: On heating, CH₃COONH₄ loses a molecule of water to give the amide: CH₃COONH₄ → CH₃CONH₂ + H₂O. No alcohol or chlorinating agent is present, so an ester or acid chloride cannot form.

questions.s: In aqueous solution near neutral pH, glycine exists mainly in the form
questions.e: The acidic –COOH group donates its proton to the basic –NH₂ group, so glycine exists as a dipolar ion (zwitterion), H₃N⁺CH₂COO⁻. The fully protonated cation forms only in strong acid, and H₂NCH₂COO⁻ only in strong alkali.

questions.s: Which carbonyl compound cannot undergo aldol condensation?
questions.e: Aldol condensation needs a hydrogen on the α-carbon (next to C=O) to form a carbanion. Methanal, HCHO, has no α-carbon at all; instead it undergoes the Cannizzaro reaction with concentrated alkali. The other three each have α-hydrogens.

questions.s: Methanal is heated with concentrated sodium hydroxide solution (Cannizzaro reaction). The products are
questions.e: In the Cannizzaro reaction one molecule of methanal is oxidised and another reduced: 2HCHO + NaOH → CH₃OH + HCOONa. No C–C bond forms, so two-carbon products such as ethanol cannot appear.

questions.s: Ethanal is warmed with acidified potassium dichromate. It is oxidised to
questions.e: Aldehydes are easily oxidised: CH₃CHO + [O] → CH₃COOH, and the dichromate turns from orange to green. Ethanol would be the reduction product, and oxidation does not change the number of carbon atoms here.

questions.s: The correct order of reactivity of carboxylic acid derivatives towards nucleophilic attack (for example hydrolysis) is
questions.e: Reactivity follows how good the leaving group is and how little it donates electrons to the C=O: Cl⁻ is the best leaving group, then RCOO⁻, then RO⁻, while –NH₂ donates strongly by resonance. So acid chloride > anhydride > ester > amide; ethanoyl chloride fumes in moist air, but amides need prolonged heating.

questions.s: Ethanal can be prepared in the laboratory by
questions.e: A primary alcohol is oxidised by acidified dichromate to an aldehyde, and ethanal is distilled off as it forms so it is not oxidised further to ethanoic acid. Propan-2-ol gives propanone, and hydrolysing the ester gives ethanol and ethanoate.

questions.s: Propyne is passed into dilute sulphuric acid containing mercury(II) sulphate. The final organic product is
questions.e: Water adds by Markovnikov's rule, putting –OH on the middle carbon to give an enol, CH₃C(OH)=CH₂, which rearranges to the ketone CH₃COCH₃. Only ethyne gives an aldehyde (ethanal) in this reaction.

questions.s: In proteins and peptides, amino acids are joined by the linkage
questions.e: The –COOH of one amino acid condenses with the –NH₂ of the next, losing water and forming the amide (peptide) link –CO–NH–. –CO–O– is the ester link found in fats and polyesters, and –O– is the glycosidic or ether link.

questions.s: Which reagent gives a precipitate with both ethanal and propanone?
questions.e: 2,4-DNPH reacts with the C=O group of any aldehyde or ketone by addition–elimination, giving an orange-yellow hydrazone precipitate. Tollens' and Fehling's reagents react only with the aldehyde, and NaHCO₃ reacts with neither.

questions.s: Which of the following polymers is made by addition polymerisation?
questions.e: PVC forms when vinyl chloride molecules, CH₂=CHCl, join through their double bonds with no small molecule lost. Nylon-6,6, terylene and proteins are condensation polymers, formed with loss of water at each link.

questions.s: Natural rubber is a polymer of
questions.e: Natural rubber is cis-polyisoprene, built from isoprene (2-methylbuta-1,3-diene) units. Ethene gives polythene, styrene gives polystyrene and vinyl chloride gives PVC, all synthetic polymers.

questions.s: Nylon-6,6 is obtained by the condensation polymerisation of
questions.e: Each –NH₂ of hexane-1,6-diamine reacts with a –COOH of hexanedioic (adipic) acid, losing water and forming amide links; both monomers have six carbons, hence 6,6. Ethane-1,2-diol with benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid gives terylene, and caprolactam gives nylon-6.

questions.s: On hydrolysis, sucrose gives
questions.e: Sucrose is a disaccharide of one glucose and one fructose unit: C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ + H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose) + C₆H₁₂O₆ (fructose). Two glucose units make maltose, and glucose with galactose makes lactose.

questions.s: Fats and oils are chemically
o: esters of glycerol with fatty acids
esters of ethanol with ethanoic acid
questions.e: Fats and oils are triglycerides: each glycerol molecule is esterified with three long-chain fatty acids. Polymers of amino acids are proteins, and polymers of glucose are starch and cellulose.

questions.s: Which nitrogenous base is found in RNA but not in DNA?
questions.e: RNA contains uracil in place of the thymine of DNA. Adenine, guanine and cytosine occur in both nucleic acids.

questions.s: The percentage of nitrogen by mass in urea, CO(NH₂)₂, is (H = 1, C = 12, N = 14, O = 16)
questions.e: Molar mass of urea = 12 + 16 + 2 × 16 = 60 g mol⁻¹, with 28 g of nitrogen, so %N = 28/60 × 100 = 46.7 %. 21.2 % is the value for ammonium sulphate, 35.0 % for ammonium nitrate and 82.4 % for ammonia itself.

questions.s: In the manufacture of Portland cement, a small amount of gypsum is ground with the clinker in order to
o: lower the melting point of clinker
slow down the setting of cement
questions.e: Without gypsum, cement mixed with water would set almost instantly; gypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O) retards the initial setting so the cement can be worked. Gypsum is added after the clinker leaves the kiln, so it cannot affect melting.

questions.s: Depletion of the ozone layer in the stratosphere is mainly caused by
questions.e: Ultraviolet light breaks C–Cl bonds in chlorofluorocarbons, releasing Cl• radicals that destroy ozone in a chain: Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂, then ClO• + O → Cl• + O₂. Carbon dioxide and methane are greenhouse gases, which is a different problem.

questions.s: Acid rain is caused mainly by the release into air of
questions.e: Sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from fuels and vehicles are oxidised and dissolve in rain to form sulphuric and nitric acids. Carbon dioxide makes rain only slightly acidic (pH about 5.6), which is normal, not acid rain.

questions.s: In a petroleum refinery, cracking of decane, C₁₀H₂₂, gives octane, C₈H₁₈, and one other product. That product is
questions.e: Balancing atoms: C₁₀H₂₂ − C₈H₁₈ = C₂H₄, which is ethene. Cracking always gives a shorter alkane plus an alkene, because there are not enough hydrogen atoms to make two alkanes; ethane, C₂H₆, would need two extra H atoms.

questions.s: Which practice follows the principles of green chemistry?
o: using large excesses of organic solvents
using catalysts in place of stoichiometric reagents
designing products that persist in the soil
choosing more toxic but cheaper reagents
questions.e: Catalysts are not used up, so they reduce waste and improve atom economy, a key green chemistry principle. Green chemistry aims to reduce solvent use, design products that break down after use, and avoid toxic substances.

questions.s: In the kraft (sulphate) process for making paper pulp, wood chips are digested with a solution of
questions.e: In the kraft process, hot sodium hydroxide and sodium sulphide dissolve the lignin that binds the cellulose fibres, leaving strong pulp. Calcium hydrogensulphite with SO₂ is used in the older sulphite process, which is the tempting wrong choice.

questions.s: Cellulose, the main material of cotton and wood, is a polymer of
questions.e: Cellulose is a long unbranched chain of β-glucose units joined by β(1→4) glycosidic links, which humans cannot digest. Starch and glycogen are the polymers of α-glucose, so α-glucose is the tempting wrong choice.

questions.s: A water sample from a river near an industrial area has a high biochemical oxygen demand (BOD). This shows that the water
o: contains a great deal of dissolved oxygen
is heavily polluted with organic matter
is very hard because of Ca²⁺ ions
questions.e: BOD measures the oxygen that microorganisms use in decomposing organic matter in the water; a high BOD means a large organic load, which leaves little oxygen for fish. Hardness from Ca²⁺ is a separate property that does not consume oxygen.
